cim_eredeti: Israel faces sovereignty threat from foreign AI control, AI chief warns
szoveg_eredeti:
Israel and other countries will lose large aspects of their sovereignty to foreign companies within five to seven years if they do not have plans in place to control the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into their infrastructure, the nation's AI Directorate chief Erez Askal said on Monday.

Speaking at the AI conference at Tel Aviv University, he warned that in the near future electricity, water, healthcare, and other sectors would be run by AI.

If the Israeli state outsources that AI to foreign multinational companies, and many of the dominators of AI globally are in the US, China, and elsewhere overseas, it could lose control of basic services critical to keeping the country running in the midst of a complex geopolitical crisis, since it will be dependent on overseas companies.

Instead, he said Israel must dash forward to develop its own AI capabilities and data centers to support those capabilities, so that it retains its independence.

Askal said that Israel would need to strike a balance of partnering with dominant AI producers overseas, while preserving control of the AI it would need to integrate into its critical infrastructure to keep up with the rest of the world and customer expectations.

Striking the right balance between rapid progress and thoughtful integration, he said, would be the main challenge of AI going forward.

In June, The Jerusalem Post reported that while Israel is considered a dominant player in the cybersecurity field, and part of that means using artificial intelligence (AI) in smart ways in that arena, in the broader AI context, Jerusalem is behind and now trying to play catch-up.

Also in June, the government approved a new wide-ranging series of AI policies which could start the rally and change the lives of all Israelis in the workplace, in education, and eventually in every area of life as the world jumps forward in this area of rapid advancement.

This decision is the culmination of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu appointing ex-9900 intelligence chief, Brig.-Gen. (res.) Erez Askal on October 12, 2025, to be the country's first AI Chief, to work alongside Israel National Cyber Directorate (INCD) Chief Yossi Karadi.

Since then, Askal has worked hard to identify the many fronts on which Israel must jump forward in its use and understanding of AI, as well as to understand how to best utilize Israel's strengths over the course of a multi-year campaign on the issue.

The Post understands that the new AI bureau's efforts have revealed that Israel's greatest strengths regarding AI are 1) Integrating and combining cybersecurity and artificial intelligence to "rub off" well on each other; and 2) Edge solutions – coming up with practical new ideas for solving problems in the field, and in war, on the front lines. These may include dealing with drones, emergency room surgery, and the classroom.

It is also considered a plus that Askal and Israel National Cyber Directorate (INCD) Chief Yossi Karadi have known each other for years from their days in Israeli intelligence, such that they can work together with no ego and without missing a beat.

From the start, Askal was given a budget of NIS 120 million, mostly for 2026, as well as 20 positions for the establishment of the directorate. Starting in 2027, NIS 13 million was due to be allocated annually for salary and operating expenses for the directorate, though Askal may decide to use the budget differently in real time than the original plans, based on the need on the ground.

The AI bureau expects that it will help: 1) Israel implement home-developed solutions and programs as opposed to requiring foreign solutions; 2) Israeli companies have products to physically manufacture from which they can make profits; 3) Pursue regulations to create order in this new area, while avoiding overregulation which stifles innovation; and 4) Mix big data and machine learning capabilities with addressing real-world problems in powerful new ways.

Following the government decision, Netanyahu said, "The purpose is clear: to establish Israel as a world leader in the area of AI because AI is not just another technology - it is a revolution. It will impact the economy, security, science, industry, health, education, and the State of Israel's international status."

Askal stated, "This decision ensures the power and achievements of Israel for the upcoming decades. In the coming years, it will become clear which countries succeed in establishing their place at the forefront of the world during the age of AI, and which will be forced to rely on the technology, infrastructure, and capabilities which others will develop."

At a conference on June 2, Askal made a major public performance, declaring, "While the great powers in the world are preoccupied with a crazy-paced arms race regarding the major layers of AI: research and development, energy, and modeling, the entire world is stuck in the embarrassing situation asking: what do we do with this tomorrow morning?"

"This is exactly where Israel's comparative advantage exists: when the giant blue Ocean of AI meets [people's] real lives. The ability to inject AI into the physical world and onto [solving] life's problems, to take an aircraft or drip irrigation and to make them 'smarter' – is a critical growth engine for us."

Some things which Askal cannot say in public due to the sensitivity of his position are that Israel had initially fallen behind in AI for a number of obvious reasons.

These include that Israel has less space to build data centers, it has fewer natural resources to cover the immense energy needs of such data centers, and its success in cybersecurity was driven in many ways by the private sector, with the government only following, whereas big AI projects need heavy government investment and interventions, which Israel's government is slower at for new projects, the Post understands.

All of this means that the AI bureau will be trying to take on a new coordinator role to facilitate the private sector working together toward clearer and more specific national AI goals, as opposed to only their own individual narrow business interests.

cim: Izrael saját AI-fejlesztések nélkül megbénulhat egy geopolitikai válságban
lead: Az izraeli AI-igazgatóság vezetője szerint az országok elveszíthetik szuverenitásukat, ha a kritikus infrastruktúrák mesterséges intelligenciáját külföldi cégeknek szervezik ki.
osszefoglalo:
Izrael és más nemzetek 5-7 éven belül **elveszíthetik szuverenitásuk jelentős részét**, ha nem veszik át az ellenőrzést az infrastruktúráikba épülő AI-rendszerek felett. Erez Askal, az izraeli AI-igazgatóság vezetője a Tel-Avivi Egyetem konferenciáján figyelmeztetett, hogy a jövőben az áram- és vízellátást, valamint az egészségügyet is algoritmusok irányítják majd. Ha ezek a rendszerek kizárólag külföldi technológiai óriásokra támaszkodnak, egy válsághelyzetben az ország működése kikerülhet a saját kezéből.

Az igazgatóság szerint a megoldás a saját adatközpontok és hazai AI-képességek gyors fejlesztése. Izrael nem versenyzik a nagyhatalmú nyelvi modellek építésében a szűkös energia- és területi erőforrásai miatt. Ehelyett a gyakorlati alkalmazásokra fókuszál: **a kiberbiztonság és az AI ötvözésére**, valamint a frontvonalakon, az egészségügyben és a mezőgazdaságban használható fizikai eszközök intelligenssé tételére.

Az izraeli kormány 120 millió sékeles büdzsével hozta létre a központi AI-hivatalt, amelynek célja a magánszektor összehangolása a nemzeti prioritásokkal. A stratégia lényege a kényes egyensúly megtalálása a külföldi AI-gyártókkal való együttműködés és a nemzetbiztonsági szempontból kritikus adatok feletti önálló ellenőrzés között.
miert_szamit: A hír rávilágít, hogy a **helyi adatbázisokra és saját infrastruktúrára épülő AI-megoldások** szerepe felértékelődik, mert a nemzetközi felhőszolgáltatóktól való teljes függőség stratégiai kockázatot jelent a cégek és intézmények számára.
